L10691: the important episodes of my life. He was not only my student in mathematics,
L10692: but also in entomology, as he started a butterfly collection after our stay at an
L10693: international conference in Boulder, Colorado. Slowly, he came to specialize in
L10694: Morphidae, and has a beautiful collection of them. For many years, we traveled
L10695: together and went butterfly hunting together. He left France for the US and
L10696: now works in Rutgers and lives in Princeton. Our families are close, particu­
L10697: larly Claudine who loves to see Francois. He is married and his two children
L10698: are now grown up. Of course, we telephone each other frequently and never
L10699: 282 A Mathematician Grappling with his Century
L10700: ## lose an occasion to make a (possibly entomological) detour when traveling.
L10701: 
L10702: He works enormously and produces remarkable articles and very pedagogical
L10703: and reputed books, for example his book on pseudo-differential operators and
L10704: Fourier integrals, which I use frequently.
L10705: Alexandre Grothendieck
L10706: The most fantastic gift to Nancy came in the person of Alexandre Grothendieck.
L10707: Bom in 1928 of a German mother, a journalist living as a refugee in France,
L10708: and a Russian anarchist, he came to France at the age of nine, shortly before
L10709: the war. His father was deported and died during the war, and his mother, to
L10710: whom he was deeply attached, worked cleaning houses in order to survive; dur­
L10711: ing the war they were interned several times in the Gurs refugee camp. To say
L10712: his secondary education was perturbed by these circumstances is of course an
L10713: understatement. However, he was able to pursue them thanks to Magnier, a high
L10714: school teacher who worked for an association helping refugees. He passed his
L10715: Licence at the University of Montpellier, without being noticed by his profes­
L10716: sors (whom he did not particularly notice either!) He then traveled to Paris in
L10717: order to become a mathematician: he wanted to work in analysis. After having
L10718: looked around a little, he went to see Cartan who advised him to come to Nancy.
L10719: We received him in October 1951. He first presented Dieudonné with an article
L10720: of about fifty pages called “Integration with values in a topological group”. It
L10721: was very precise, but not at all interesting. Dieudonné displayed his character­
L10722: istic - ephemeral - aggressivity and scolded him energetically, telling him that
L10723: generalizing for the pure pleasure of generalizing was no way to work. One
L10724: should attack difficult problems which could then have applications in the rest
L10725: of mathematics, or in other sciences: the results in his article would never be of
L10726: any use to anyone. Dieudonné was right, although Grothendieck never admitted
L10727: it. However, Dieudonné did not give up on him. He and I had just published an
L10728: article on “The spaces 9 and Distributions had started up a whole series
L10729: of new topological vector spaces, above all the space 3) of C00 functions with

L10889: written. Generally, publications are not very time-resistant, and it is necessary to
L10890: rewrite them or have them rewritten. But the book on distributions has withstood
L10891: the test of time. I believe that for the most part, I introduced the best possible
L10892: definitions and proofs.
L10893: This was my working schedule at the University of Nancy. Every morning,
L10894: I worked on pure research - not distributions - on all kinds of subjects, and
L10895: in the afternoons, I wrote up distributions. The combination of these two tasks
L10896: Chapter VII: Militating, Teaching, Research 287
L10897: and the need for scrupulous technical rigor caused me to advance rather slowly.
L10898: Gel’fand’s book on generalized functions only appeared in 1955. I devoted so
L10899: much time to research that if I did not pay attention, I started to suffer from
L10900: overwork. To avoid that, I finished every afternoon with a non-mathematical
L10901: activity. I also thought about varied subjects, often inspired by the Saturday
L10902: seminars in Nancy. Before Nancy, I had thought about potential theory, with
L10903: Brelot in Grenoble and thanks to an article of Cartan which I read. In our
L10904: Saturday seminar, we had talks on spectral decomposition, representations of
L10905: compact groups (Peter-Weyl), a few rather poor ideas on representations of lo­
L10906: cally compact groups, without Harish-Chandra’s theory. We studied Dixmier’s
L10907: direct sums of Hilbert spaces and his trace theorems, and von Neumann’s clas­
L10908: sification of algebras into types I, II and III. Lie algebras and Lie groups were
L10909: also studied. I was very interested in them and wrote up the version zero of the
L10910: book on Lie groups for Bourbaki in the fifties. Once, I was dictating a letter to
L10911: Dieudonné to my secretary and I said “Lie groups (groupes de Lie) prevent me
L10912: from sleeping” which she transcribed “Groups of beds (groupes de fits) prevent
L10913: me from sleeping”, which is, after all, no less logical. (Another time, when I
L10914: dictated “théorie quantique des champs” she wrote, always with logic, “théorie
L10915: cantique des chants”). However, I never studied their classification and know
L10916: almost nothing about exceptional Lie groups. Dieudonné worked on Dedekind
L10917: number fields and p-adic fields, adeles and ideles. We also studied algebraic
L10918: topology. After the publication of a famous little book by Cartan and Eilenberg
L10919: called New Methods in Algebraic Topology, the use of exact sequences became
